title: Franz Jägerstätter (1907–1943)
hookLine: an Austrian farmer refuses to fight for Hitler and is executed

cards: A village in the Austrian hills. When Austria is joined to Hitler's Germany, the people vote on it, and the result in his village is yes. One farmer votes no.
He's not a priest or a professor. Franz Jägerstätter farms, with a wife named Franziska and young daughters.
In the war years he also becomes the sacristan at the parish church, ringing the bell and setting out the vessels for Mass. Then a call-up letter orders him to report for duty.
He reports, and he tells them he will not fight.

teach.b: First, the conscience. Franz had thought it through, in prayer and on paper. He believed the Nazi cause was evil, and that fighting for it would be a sin he could not commit.
Second, the advice. He was not cheered on.

His parish priest and his bishop urged him to serve, for the sake of his family, telling him the responsibility belonged to those who gave the orders. People in the village thought he was throwing his life away.
He listened to them with respect, and still said no. Third, the prison. He was arrested, tried and sentenced to death.
In his cell he wrote letters to Franziska, full of love for her and the girls, and notes on why he could not do what he was told. Franziska stood by him. Fourth, the scaffold.

He was executed, and for years some in his village and his Church treated him as a man who had abandoned his family. Later, the Church beatified him as a martyr, with Franziska still living to see it.

teach.h: WE OUGHT TO OBEY GOD, RATHER THAN MEN.
teach.b: The apostles told the authorities in Acts, in the Douay-Rheims: "We ought to obey God, rather than men." Franz took that line seriously, even against the advice of those he trusted.

This week ran from a pope who called a war a useless slaughter, through a friar's confessional, a sister's diary, Kolbe's presses, Edith Stein and the hard record of the Holocaust, to a farmer who said no.

how: Catholics honor Blessed Franz Jägerstätter as a martyr of conscience; his village parish and Catholic peace groups keep his memory with prayer and readings from his prison letters.

games.q: you're called up to fight for a cause you believe is evil. your priest, your bishop and your neighbors all say serve, for your family's sake. what do you do?
o: serve, and leave the blame to those giving orders.
run and hide in the hills.
games.why: he reported and refused. he was tried and executed, and the Church later beatified him as a martyr.

practice: Ask yourself quietly where you're going along with something you know isn't right: a joke at someone's expense, a shortcut at work, a silence when something should be said.
Don't pick the biggest thing; pick a small one, the size of one vote in one village, and picture what saying no would look like. If you pray, ask for courage.
